title: The log at the centre
teaches: Append-only partitioned logs, offsets and consumer groups, ordering by key, retention and replay, and why sequential disk is fast

blocks.text: By 2010 LinkedIn ran a dozen or so systems that each held part of what its members did: Oracle databases for profiles and connections, a search index, a social graph service, a Hadoop cluster, a data warehouse, monitoring, a recommendation system. Each needed data from several of the others, and each connection was a pipeline someone had written by hand: a nightly dump, a script that polled a table, a feed in some format only two teams understood. Jay Kreps, who worked on the infrastructure, later drew it as a tangle of arrows between boxes, and said a large share of the team's time went into keeping those arrows working.[^name]

The arithmetic is unkind. With *n* systems that each read from each other, there can be *n*(*n* − 1) pipelines; ten systems allow ninety. Each pipeline breaks in its own way, carries its own format, and copies the data at its own speed, so two systems that should agree drift apart. Worse, much of the data was not database rows at all but **activity**: page views, searches, clicks, ads shown. Activity outnumbers database writes by orders of magnitude, and it was arriving faster every month.

Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao built a system to sit in the middle. Every source writes its data once, to one place; every system that wants it reads from that place, at its own pace, and neither side needs to know the other exists. The habit here is that move: **decouple** the writers from the readers by putting something durable between them. They called it Kafka, described it in a paper at the NetDB workshop in Athens in June 2011, and released it as open source that year. The paper reports that LinkedIn was already collecting hundreds of gigabytes and close to a billion messages a day through it.[^scale]

parts.title: A file you only append to

blocks.text: Kafka's central data structure is a **log**: an ordered sequence of records that can only be added to at the end. Nothing in it is changed or deleted one record at a time. Each record gets a number, its **offset**, one more than the record before. A database keeps a log like this for its own recovery (lesson 15's mcsqueal read MySQL's); Kafka makes the log the product.

Data is grouped into named **topics**, such as page views or clicks. A topic is split into **partitions**, and each partition is a separate log, kept on one machine (a **broker**) and numbered from offset 0. On disk a partition is a directory of **segment** files, each about a gigabyte, named by the first offset it holds. A record is appended to the newest segment; old segments are closed and, after a set time such as seven days, deleted whole. Beside each segment is a small, sparse index from offset to byte position, so a read can start anywhere. Retention sets the disk: 10,000 messages a second of 1 KB is 10 MB/s, and seven days of it is 10 MB/s × 604,800 s, about 6 TB, or 18 TB with three copies.

blocks.caption: One partition on a broker's disk: segment files named by their first offset, and a sparse index for each. Sizes are typical; offsets are made up. A read for an offset finds its segment by file name, then the nearest earlier entry in that segment's index, then scans forward a few kilobytes.

blocks.text: On the wire, a **producer** sends a batch of records for a partition to the broker that holds it, which appends them and acknowledges. A **consumer** asks the broker for "partition 2 of clicks from offset 2,079,881, up to a megabyte" and gets back the bytes of the segment from that point. That request is the whole reading protocol. The broker does not track what each consumer has read, and it does not delete a record when it is read. A record stays until its segment ages out, however many consumers have read it, or none.

Those two choices are what make the decoupling work. A consumer that falls an hour behind costs the broker nothing; it just asks for older offsets. A new system that wants the last week of clicks starts at the oldest offset and reads forward. A consumer with a bug can be fixed and wound back to yesterday's offset to process the day again.

parts.title: Why a disk can be fast

blocks.text: Keeping every message on disk sounds slow; the message queues of 2010 worked hard to keep messages in memory. Lesson 1 put a disk seek at about 10 ms. A design that writes each 1 KB message to its own place on a hard disk pays a seek each time: about 100 messages, 0.1 MB, a second per disk. The same disk writing to the end of one file never seeks, and streams at 100 MB/s or more: about 100,000 messages a second. By this estimate the order of the writes is worth a factor of about a thousand.

blocks.caption: The same disks written at random and in order, with an NVMe SSD and main memory for comparison, on a scale where each mark is ten times the last. Kafka's design notes give the first pair; the others are round figures for the 2020s. The first two bars are the same disks; only the order of the writes differs.

blocks.text: Kafka's documentation reports six 7,200 rpm disks in a RAID-5 array taking about 600 MB/s of writes in order and about 100 KB/s at random, a factor of over 6,000. The measured factor is larger than the estimate because six disks add up their speed when streaming, and in RAID-5 each small random write costs several disk operations, to update the parity. Appending is the order the disk is good at. Reading is mostly in order too, because consumers read forward from where they were.

Three more choices did the rest. Kafka keeps no cache of its own; it writes to files and lets the operating system's **page cache** hold recent data in spare memory, so a consumer that is keeping up reads what was just written without touching the disk. It sends batches, so one network request and one disk write carry hundreds of messages. And it sends a segment's bytes to the network with the operating system's `sendfile` call, straight from the page cache to the socket, without copying them through the broker's own memory.[^zerocopy] The paper measured one broker taking about 50,000 small messages a second sent one at a time and about 400,000 a second in batches of 50, several times what the queues it compared against managed.

Order is kept within a partition and nowhere else. Two records in partition 0 are read in the order they were written; a record in partition 0 and one in partition 3 have no order at all. So a producer chooses the partition by a **key**: the partition is a hash of the key, modulo the number of partitions, and every record with the same key lands in the same partition, in order.

Choosing the key is choosing what must stay in order. For a bank's account events, key by account: a deposit and the withdrawal after it must be applied in that order, and two different accounts can go in any order. For page views being counted, any key will do, and spreading them evenly matters more. Two designs fail here. Spreading records at random looks balanced and quietly reorders each account's events. Putting everything in one partition keeps a total order and caps the topic at what one broker and one consumer can do.

Partitions are also the unit of parallel reading, which sets their number. Within a group of consumers sharing the work (next part), each partition is read by exactly one consumer at a time. If a topic takes 60,000 messages a second and one consumer can process 4,000 a second, the topic needs at least 15 partitions for the group to keep up, and a few times that leaves room to grow, since adding partitions later changes which partition each key hashes to. After the change a key's new records go to a different partition from its old ones, and a reader can see a newer record before an older one it has not reached yet. To grow without breaking per-key order, either start with enough partitions, or create a new topic with more and move writers and then readers over at a known point. More is not free: each partition is a set of open files, a leader to elect, and data to replicate, and a hot key still lands on one partition however many there are.

A **consumer group** is a set of consumers that share a topic's work: the group's partitions are dealt among its members, and each member reads its partitions forward. Each group keeps its own position in every partition, and from time to time each member **commits** its position, writing down "I have processed partition 2 up to offset 2,079,950". Different groups never interfere: billing, fraud detection and the data warehouse can each read every click, at their own pace.

The gap between the newest offset in a partition and a group's position is the group's **lag**, in messages. Lag is the first number to watch on any log: it stays small and steady while the group keeps up, and grows when the group is too slow or a member is gone.

blocks.caption: A topic of six partitions read by a group of three consumers. Tap a consumer to stop it. Rates are slowed down to be followed by eye.
blocks.task: Stop a consumer, let its partitions move, then get the group's lag back under 10

blocks.text: When a consumer stops answering, the group notices after a **session timeout** (a few seconds; the figure uses 2) and **rebalances**: its partitions are dealt to the members left. The new owner starts each partition at the last committed offset, because that is all it knows. Messages the dead consumer had processed but not yet committed are processed a second time. This is the delivery guarantee a log gives a consumer, **at least once**: nothing is skipped, and anything may be seen twice. Committing more often shrinks the repeats but never removes them, since a consumer can always die between doing the work and writing down that it did. A consumer has to tolerate repeats; lesson 17 makes that exact.

The button that adds a reader from offset 0 is replay. The new reader starts with the whole retained history behind it, reads it far faster than it arrives, and then keeps up like anyone else. This is how a new search index, a new cache or a fixed version of a buggy job gets built: from the log, not from a special export.[^offsets]

A traditional message queue (RabbitMQ, Amazon SQS) works differently. Each message is handed to one worker, the worker acknowledges it, and then it is deleted. A message whose worker fails is handed to another worker on its own, with no partition to stall, and one that fails over and over can be set aside in a **dead-letter queue**. That suits a pile of independent jobs: send these emails, resize these photos. A log has no dead-letter queue of its own: a consumer that cannot process a message must write it to a separate topic of failures and move on, or its whole partition stalls behind that one message. A queue does not keep history, and two systems that each want every message need two queues and a copy. A log keeps everything for its retention period, lets any number of groups read it, and keeps order per key, at the cost of handing out work a whole partition at a time.

The figure below has six jobs to place: feed every click to billing, fraud checks and the warehouse; send each welcome email once, from whichever worker is free; build a new search index from every profile edit so far; transcode 10,000 uploaded videos, some taking an hour; apply each account's payments in the order they were made; and retry a failed image resize, then set it aside after five tries.

items.why: A new search index built from every profile edit so far is a replay from the oldest offset; a queue would have deleted the history.

items.name: Hour-long video jobs
items.why: Transcoding 10,000 uploads, some taking an hour: long, uneven jobs handed out one at a time; a log would stall a partition behind the slowest.

items.name: Payments in order
items.why: Each account's payments must be applied in the order made. Key by account and each account's records stay in order in one partition.

items.name: Retry, then park
items.why: A failed image resize retried, then set aside after five tries. Per-message acknowledgement, redelivery and a dead-letter queue are what queues do.

blocks.text: The log also answers a problem that every system with a database and a message stream meets: the **dual write**. A service saves an order to its database, then publishes "order placed" to Kafka. If it crashes between the two, the database has the order and nobody else will ever hear of it; publish first and crash, and everyone hears of an order that does not exist. No ordering of two separate writes fixes this. Lesson 22 shows one cure, the outbox. Kreps argued for the other: make the log the record of what happened, and build the database, the caches and the search index by reading it, as lesson 15's caches were kept fresh by reading MySQL's log. Copying a database's own change log into Kafka, called **change data capture**, is how that is usually done with an existing database.

The 2011 Kafka kept each partition on one broker; if its disk died, the partition's data went with it. Replication arrived in version 0.8 in 2013: each partition has a leader broker that takes writes and followers that copy them, and a producer can wait until every follower that is in step has the record before counting it written. A follower is in step, an **in-sync replica**, while it has fetched everything up to the leader's newest record within a set time, 10 seconds by default for many years and 30 seconds since version 2.5; one that falls further behind is dropped from the set until it catches up. Retention also grew a second mode, **compaction**, which keeps only the newest record for each key, so a topic can serve as the full current state of a table, however old.[^compaction]

blocks.caption: Seven questions on logs, partitions and consumers
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A consumer group's lag on a topic grows steadily all afternoon. What does that tell you?
choices: The group reads more slowly than producers write, so it needs faster or more consumers, and partitions to spread them over
The brokers are deleting old segments before the group has read them, so the group has to keep starting again from the beginning
The producers are sending duplicate messages, which the group has to read and then discard one by one
items.why: Lag is the newest offset minus the group's position. Steady growth means arrivals exceed the group's rate. More consumers help only up to one per partition.

items.ask: Events for each bank account must be applied in the order they happened. How should they be written to a partitioned log?
choices: Spread evenly over all partitions at random, and sort each account's events by timestamp when they are read
With the account number as the key, so all of one account's events go to one partition in order
All to a single partition, since that is the only way a log can keep any events in order
items.why: Order holds only within a partition. Keying by account keeps each account in order and still spreads accounts over partitions. Timestamps from many machines do not give a reliable order, and one partition caps throughput.

items.ask: A topic takes 60,000 messages a second. One consumer can process 4,000 a second. What is the least number of partitions for one group to keep up?
items.why: Each partition is read by one consumer in a group, so the group can use at most one consumer per partition: 60,000 / 4,000 = 15 consumers, so at least 15 partitions.

items.ask: A consumer crashes and its partitions move to another member of its group. Why are some messages processed twice?
choices: The broker resends every message the crashed consumer was sent, in case its acknowledgements were lost on the way
The new owner starts from the last committed offset, and the crashed one had processed some messages after committing
Producers retry when a consumer crashes, so the messages it was handling are appended to the log a second time
items.why: Work and commit are two steps; a crash between them leaves processed but uncommitted messages, which the next owner reads again. That is at-least-once delivery.

items.ask: Why can Kafka keep every message on disk and still be fast?
choices: Writes append and reads run forward, so the disk streams instead of seeking, and recent data comes from the page cache
It keeps each partition entirely in memory and writes to disk only during quiet periods when no producer is sending anything
It compresses each message so heavily that the disk has very little to write, whatever order the writes come in
items.why: Writes in order on a hard disk run hundreds or thousands of times faster than random ones. The operating system's page cache holds what was just written, and batching and sendfile cut the per-message cost.

items.ask: Which job suits a task queue better than a partitioned log?
choices: Letting a new analytics system read the last week of sign-ups from the beginning
Handing thousands of independent hour-long video transcodes to whichever worker is free
Feeding the same stream of clicks to billing, fraud detection and a data warehouse
items.why: Long, uneven, independent jobs want per-message hand-out and acknowledgement. In a log, one slow message holds up its whole partition for that group. The other two need replay and several readers, which a log gives.

items.ask: A service writes an order to its database and then publishes an event about it to a log. What can go wrong?
choices: Nothing, as long as the publish is retried until the log acknowledges it
The log may deliver the event to its readers before the database has finished committing the order itself
A crash between the two writes leaves the database and the log disagreeing, with no record of the gap
items.why: Two separate writes can be split by a crash in either order. The cures are an outbox written in the same transaction, or making the log the source and building the database from it.

summary: **Put a durable log between writers and readers.** Each source writes once and each reader reads at its own pace, instead of a hand-built pipeline for every pair.
**A log is append-only and addressed by offset.** Kafka keeps a topic as partitions, each a directory of segment files on one broker, and deletes whole segments by age.
**Writing in order is what makes disk fast.** Appends stream at hundreds of MB/s where random writes manage well under one, and the page cache serves recent reads.
**Order holds only within a partition.** Key records by what must stay in order (an account, a user), and the key's hash picks the partition.
**Partitions set the parallelism.** A group uses at most one consumer per partition, so rate divided by one consumer's speed gives the least number of partitions.
**Lag is the number to watch.** It is the newest offset minus the group's position, and it grows when readers are slower than writers.
**A log delivers at least once.** After a rebalance a partition restarts from its last committed offset, so consumers must tolerate repeats.
**Replay builds new systems from history.** A new reader starts at the oldest retained offset and catches up.
**Avoid dual writes.** A database write and a separate publish can be split by a crash; use an outbox or build the database from the log.

name.title: Why Kafka
name.text: Kreps later explained the name: since this was a system built for writing, a writer's name seemed to fit, and he liked Franz Kafka's work. Kreps's 2013 essay "The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction" made the case for the design at length.

scale.title: From a billion to trillions
scale.text: LinkedIn's reported volume passed a trillion messages a day by the middle of the 2010s. Kreps, Narkhede and Rao left LinkedIn in 2014 to found a company, Confluent, around it.

zerocopy.title: sendfile
zerocopy.text: A plain server reads file bytes into its own memory and then writes them to a socket: two copies across the boundary between the program and the kernel, plus system calls for each. Linux's `sendfile` asks the kernel to move bytes from a file straight to a socket. It works for Kafka because the broker stores records in the same format it sends them in, and never needs to look inside.

offsets.title: Where offsets are kept
offsets.text: In the 2011 design, consumers stored their committed offsets in ZooKeeper (a coordination service like lesson 11's Chubby). Later versions keep them in an internal Kafka topic of their own, and a broker acting as group coordinator runs the rebalances.

compaction.title: Compaction
compaction.text: A compacted topic is cleaned in the background: for each key, older records are dropped once a newer one exists, and a record with an empty value deletes its key. A reader that starts at offset 0 still sees every key's latest value, so the topic can rebuild a table or a cache from scratch.
